items.label: practice
items.t: Leaving with an even mind when the hour that cannot be avoided comes has to be learned over a long time. I practise every day so that I can leave life with an even mind, instead of clasping life as people swept away by rushing water clasp thorns and jagged edges.
items.why: Marcus’s practice here is to look at the people I am leaving, at the hour itself. Seneca adds that the even mind has to be learned long before, by practising it every day.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is a great thing, Lucilius, and one that has to be learned over a long time: to go away with an even mind when that hour which cannot be avoided draws near.
support.follows: To leave life with an even mind when the hour comes is a great thing, and it has to be learned over a long time.
support.context: Letter 30: Seneca admires his old friend Bassus, who faces his own death with a calm face. Here “that hour which cannot be avoided” is the hour of death.
gives: Leaving with an even mind when the hour that cannot be avoided comes has to be learned over a long time

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Practise this every day, so that you can leave life with an even mind: life, which many clasp and hold on to in the way that people being swept away by rushing water clasp thorns and jagged edges.
support.follows: Practising this every day lets one leave life with an even mind instead of holding on to it.
support.context: Letter 4, on the terrors of death. “Practise this” points to the thought just before it: no one lives in peace who thinks too much about making life longer.
gives: I practise every day so that I can leave life with an even mind
instead of clasping life as people swept away by rushing water clasp thorns and jagged edges

items.label: breaks
items.t: Failing can also mean wanting death. I do not flee from life or let a longing for death take hold of me; if I run to death out of weariness of life, it is the way I live that has made the running necessary.
items.why: Marcus names fear as the failure. Seneca names the opposite one, a longing for death. In 9.3 Marcus touches it in “Come sooner, death”, a sentence this article leaves out, and perhaps in “nor violent”, which the translators note may mean pushing toward death.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it. And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying.
support.follows: A wise person does not flee from life but goes out of it, and guards against the longing for death.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death. Seneca warns that despising death can turn into wanting it: fleeing from life, even when reason seems to advise an end.
gives: I do not flee from life or let a longing for death take hold of me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: to run to death out of weariness of life, when it is by your way of life that you have made it necessary to run to death
support.follows: Whoever runs to death out of weariness of life has made that running necessary by the way he lives.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca quotes Epicurus, who rebukes those who long for death no less than those who fear it, and calls this running ridiculous.
gives: if I run to death out of weariness of life, it is the way I live that has made the running necessary

items.label: doubt
items.t: Death either consumes me or strips me bare. If it lets me out, better things remain for me, with the burden taken off; if it consumes me, nothing remains, neither good nor bad, and that is no different from never having begun.
items.why: 8.55 argues from sensation: none, or a different kind. Seneca’s two cases are about what remains for me, better things or nothing, and he likens nothing to the time before I was born.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Death either consumes us or strips us bare. For those who are let out, better things remain, with the burden taken off; for those who are consumed, nothing remains: good things and bad alike have been removed.
support.follows: If death lets us out, better things remain, with the burden taken off; if it consumes us, nothing remains, good or bad.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death, after dismissing the fears of the underworld as fit only for children. “The burden” is the body.
gives: Death either consumes me or strips me bare
If it lets me out, better things remain for me, with the burden taken off
if it consumes me, nothing remains, neither good nor bad

support.author: seneca
support.quote: for what does it matter whether you do not begin or you cease, when the result of both is this, not to be?
support.follows: Not beginning and ceasing have the same result, not to be, so it does not matter which.
support.context: Letter 54, written after an attack of asthma: we are lit and put out like a lamp. By “both” he means the time before birth and the time after death.

items.t: Seneca counts death indifferent: not an evil, but not a good either. It still keeps a look of evil, because we love ourselves, want to go on existing and recoil from dissolution, so we cannot easily disregard it and the mind must be hardened by much training to bear its approach. This limits claim 3 rather than contradicting it: Marcus calls death good only when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole (12.17), and Seneca speaks of death in itself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: death is among those things that are not indeed evils, yet have the look of an evil
support.follows: Death is not an evil, but it still looks like one.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death. Seneca explains why death, though indifferent, is feared: love of self and a recoil from dissolution are born in us.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: even if death is a matter of indifference, it is still not a thing that can easily be disregarded: the mind must be hardened by much training to bear the sight of it and its approach.
support.follows: Death is neither good nor bad, yet it cannot easily be disregarded, and the mind must be hardened by much training to bear its approach.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death: Seneca’s conclusion from the recoil from dissolution that is born in us, and what it asks of us in practice.

items.t: Seneca does not let the people I leave be only a reason to go. My own people can be a reason to stay: a good man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he pleases, and holds on to life even with torment when they need him. This limits claim 5; 9.3 too allows that living with people of one’s own principles would hold one in life.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: sometimes, even if there are pressing reasons, the breath must be called back, even with torment, out of regard for one’s own people, and held back in the very mouth
support.follows: Sometimes, out of regard for our own people, we must hold on to life even when it costs us torment.
support.context: Letter 104: Seneca, old and ill, has weighed letting himself die, and keeps himself alive for his wife Paulina. She is among “one’s own people”.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: since the good man must live not as long as it pleases him but as long as he ought.
support.follows: A good man lives as long as he ought to, not as long as he likes.
support.context: Letter 104, on Seneca keeping himself alive for his wife Paulina: the reason he gives for holding on to life for those one loves.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: We die every day; for every day some part of life is taken away, and even at the time when we are growing, life is growing less. We have lost infancy, then childhood, then youth. Right up to yesterday, whatever time has passed has perished; this very day that we are living we share with death. Just as it is not the last drop that empties a water clock but whatever has run out before, so the last hour, in which we cease to be, does not alone make death but alone completes it. That is when we come to it, but we have been coming for a long time.

passages.title: On an old man's calm before death
passages.text: You may count Bassus among these, a man who did not want us to be deceived. He says that a man who fears death is as much a fool as one who fears old age; for just as old age follows youth, so death follows old age. Whoever does not want to die did not want to live; for life was given with death as its proviso; it is towards death that one goes. To fear it is what a madman does, for this reason: what is certain is waited for, what is doubtful is feared.

passages.title: On an old man's calm before death
passages.text: This is a great thing, Lucilius, and one that has to be learned over a long time: to go away with an even mind when that hour which cannot be avoided draws near. Other kinds of death are mixed with hope: an illness comes to an end, a fire is put out, a falling building has set down the people it seemed about to crush; the sea has thrown out unharmed those it had swallowed, with the same force with which it was sucking them down; a soldier has drawn his sword back from the very neck of the man who was about to die. The man whom old age is leading to death has nothing to hope for; against this alone no one can step in. By no kind of death do people die more gently, but by none more slowly either.

passages.title: On overcoming the fear of death
passages.text: Practise this every day, so that you can leave life with an even mind: life, which many clasp and hold on to in the way that people being swept away by rushing water clasp thorns and jagged edges. Most people are tossed about, wretched, between the fear of death and the torments of life, and they do not want to live, they do not know how to die.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it. And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying. For there is, my Lucilius, as towards other things, so also towards dying, an unconsidered leaning of the mind, which often seizes men who are noble and of the keenest character, and often the spiritless and the downcast. The former scorn life; the latter find it a burden.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: I see what you are looking for: you are asking what I have packed into this letter, what spirited saying of someone’s, what useful precept. Something will be sent from this very subject, the one that has been in hand. Epicurus rebukes those who long for death no less than those who fear it, and says: “It is ridiculous to run to death out of weariness of life, when it is by your way of life that you have made it necessary to run to death.”

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: I am not so silly as to go through the Epicurean refrain at this point and say that the fears of the underworld are empty, that Ixion is not turned on a wheel, that no rock is pushed uphill by the shoulders of Sisyphus, that no one’s entrails can both grow back and be torn at every day. No one is so much a child as to fear Cerberus and the darkness and the ghostly look of those whose bare bones hang together. Death either consumes us or strips us bare. For those who are let out, better things remain, with the burden taken off; for those who are consumed, nothing remains: good things and bad alike have been removed.

passages.title: On asthma and rehearsing death
passages.text: I ask you, would you not call it most foolish if someone thought that a lamp is worse off when it has been put out than before it is lit? We too are both put out and lit: in the time between we go through something, but on either side there is deep freedom from care. For this, my Lucilius, unless I am mistaken, is where we go wrong: we judge that death follows, when it has both gone before and will follow. Whatever was before us is death; for what does it matter whether you do not begin or you cease, when the result of both is this, not to be?

passages.title: On facing death without logical tricks
passages.text: Among these things too, Lucilius, which we call middle, there is a great difference. For death is not a matter of indifference in the same way as whether you have an even number of hairs: death is among those things that are not indeed evils, yet have the look of an evil. There is love of self, and an inborn will to last and to preserve oneself, and a shrinking from dissolution, [gap in the Latin text] because it seems to snatch many goods away from us and to lead us out of this plenty of things to which we have grown used. This too estranges us from death, that we already know the things here, while we do not know what the things are like to which we are going to cross over, and we shudder at the unknown. Besides, there is a natural fear of the dark, into which, it is believed, death will lead us.

passages.title: On facing death without logical tricks
passages.text: So even if death is a matter of indifference, it is still not a thing that can easily be disregarded: the mind must be hardened by much training to bear the sight of it and its approach. Death ought to be scorned more than it usually is; for we have believed many things about it; the talents of many have competed to increase its bad name; a prison in the underworld has been described, and a region weighed down by everlasting night, in which the huge doorkeeper of Orcus, lying on half-eaten bones in his bloody cave, barking for ever, frightens the bloodless shades. Even when you have persuaded people that these are stories and that nothing is left for the dead to fear, another fear comes up: for they are equally afraid of being in the underworld and of being nowhere.

passages.title: On travel, health and the examples of great men
passages.text: For one must indulge honourable feelings; and sometimes, even if there are pressing reasons, the breath must be called back, even with torment, out of regard for one’s own people, and held back in the very mouth, since the good man must live not as long as it pleases him but as long as he ought. The man who thinks neither a wife nor a friend worth so much that he would stay longer in life, who will persist in dying, is soft. This too the mind should command of itself, when the interest of its own people demands it: not only if it wants to die but if it has begun to, it should pause and oblige its own people.

claims.t: Dying is one of nature’s works, and it is also good for nature.
claims.shared: Three passages say that death is one of nature’s things: 9.3 “one of the things nature wills”, 10.36 “one of the things that accord with nature”, 2.10 “a work of nature”. 9.3 and 10.36 even share the words “this too is one of the things”.
claims.changed: The claim uses 2.10’s word, “work”, for all three. Only 2.10 adds that death is also good for nature.

support.quote: since this too is one of the things nature wills
support.follows: Death too is one of the things that nature wills.
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works

support.quote: for this too is one of the things that accord with nature
support.follows: Being untied from my own people at death, without being pulled back, is one of the things that accord with nature.
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works

support.quote: This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.
support.follows: Dying is a work of nature, and it is also good for nature.
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works
it is also good for nature

claims.t: I have already lived through many small deaths: activities that stopped, and ages of my life that gave way to the next. None of them was bad, and neither is the ending of my whole life.
claims.shared: 9.19 and 12.17 both say that the ending of an activity is “nothing bad” and that, “in the same way”, neither is the ending of a whole life. 9.3 and 9.19 both name the ages of life (being young and growing old; childhood, youth, old age) as changes of the same kind as dying; 9.19 calls each of them “a death”.
claims.changed: 12.17 adds “at the right time” to both endings; the claim leaves the time to claim 3. 9.19 says the changes are “nothing terrible”, 12.17 that they suffer “nothing bad”; the claim says “bad”. 9.3 also names teeth, beard, grey hair and childbirth, and 9.19 the stages of a life under grandfather, mother and father; the claim keeps the ages. “Small deaths” is the editor’s word for 9.19’s “every change of these too is a death”.

support.quote: For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved.
support.follows: Dying is a change like growing old, getting grey hair or giving birth: one of the natural activities the seasons of life bring.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next

support.quote: The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad.
support.follows: When an activity, an impulse or a judgment ends, nothing bad has happened.
gives: activities that stopped
None of them was bad

support.quote: Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible?
support.follows: Each passage from one age of life to the next is a kind of death, and none of them is terrible.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next
I have already lived through many small deaths
None of them was bad

support.quote: In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.
support.follows: The ending of my whole life is no more terrible than the smaller endings before it.
gives: neither is the ending of my whole life

support.quote: Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped
support.follows: An activity that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad by having stopped.
gives: activities that stopped
None of them was bad

support.quote: In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped
support.follows: A life, the sum of a person’s actions, suffers nothing bad by stopping, if it stops at the right time.
gives: neither is the ending of my whole life

claims.t: It is nature, not a tyrant or an unjust judge, that sends me away, and nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit. My death is not a bad thing, and when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole, it is a good one.
claims.shared: 12.17 and 12.27 both say that the end of a life is fixed by another and not by me: “The right time and the limit are given by nature”; “what is complete is fixed by the one who … ; you are responsible for neither”.
claims.changed: 12.27 names nature as the one who sends me away, then says what is complete is fixed by “the one” responsible for the putting together and the dissolving, a masculine word in the Greek (god, or the magistrate of the image); the claim calls it nature, as 12.17 does. 12.27 does not say whose putting together and dissolving is meant; the claim reads them as mine, from “you are responsible for neither”, and keeps only that the limit is not my doing. 12.17 says death is not bad “if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial”; the claim drops that condition, and “not I” stands in for its first half.

support.quote: sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in
support.follows: It is nature, which brought me into life, that sends me out of it, not a tyrant or an unjust judge.
gives: It is nature, not a tyrant or an unjust judge, that sends me away

support.quote: For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither.
support.follows: What is complete is fixed by the one responsible for the putting together and the dissolving, and neither is my doing.
gives: nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit

support.quote: The right time and the limit are given by nature
support.follows: It is nature that gives the right time and the limit of a life.
gives: nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit

support.quote: So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole.
support.follows: If it is not chosen and not against the community, the end of a life is not shameful and so not bad; it is good when it comes at the right time for the whole.
gives: My death is not a bad thing
when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole, it is a good one

claims.t: When my death comes I go graciously, not as one torn away, and with goodwill toward the people I leave.
claims.shared: 12.27 and 10.36 both tell the one who is dying to “go away” and to be “gracious” (the same Greek word in both). 9.3 and 10.36 both ask for goodwill toward the people left behind: “care for them and bear with them gently”, “friendly, well-disposed and gracious”.
claims.changed: In 12.27 one goes graciously because the one who dismisses is gracious; in 10.36 one stays gracious toward the people who want one gone. The claim keeps the manner and drops both reasons. 9.3’s waiting for death and being well pleased with it are left to Article 10, which says them.

support.quote: So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.
support.follows: I should leave graciously, since the one who dismisses me is gracious too.
gives: I go graciously

support.quote: Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly toward them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.
support.follows: Even toward people who are glad to see me go, I should leave as I always was with them: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.
gives: I go graciously
with goodwill toward the people I leave

support.quote: not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, such too must the withdrawal from these people be.
support.follows: I should leave the people of my life not as one torn away, but as easily as the soul slips from the body in an easy death.
gives: not as one torn away

support.quote: rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently
support.follows: One must care for the people one is leaving and bear with them gently.
gives: with goodwill toward the people I leave

claims.t: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving. They do not share my principles, and even those I struggled for want me to go; there is nothing here to hold on to.
claims.shared: 9.3 and 10.36 both give the same help for dying: look at the people you are leaving and you will go more easily (9.3 “put you at ease”, 10.36 “go out more easily”). Both end on what would “hold” one in life: 9.3 only the company of people with the same principles, 10.36 nothing, since even one’s partners want one gone.
claims.changed: 9.3 calls this a layman’s rule and adds that one must not take offence at these people; 10.36 says that even a good and wise person has someone glad to see him go. The claim keeps the looking and what it shows, and leaves the goodwill to claim 4. 9.3e says “the things you are about to leave”; the people are read from the words the edition restores in brackets for a gap (“[at what kind of] characters”) and from the “them” that follows, and the translators’ note leaves open whether “the things” include people.

support.quote: what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave
support.follows: What most eases a person about death is to stop and look at what they are about to leave.
gives: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving

support.quote: So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, took thought, those very people want me to go
support.follows: Dying, I will go more easily if I remember that even the partners I struggled and prayed for want me to go.
gives: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving
even those I struggled for want me to go

support.quote: remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you
support.follows: The people death releases me from are not people who share my principles.
gives: They do not share my principles

support.quote: For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own.
support.follows: The one thing that could hold a person in life is living with people who share their principles.
gives: there is nothing here to hold on to

support.quote: Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?
support.follows: There is no reason to hold on to a longer stay in such a life.
gives: there is nothing here to hold on to

single.quote: Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.
single.label: A rest
single.t: Death is a rest: from the impacts on my senses, from being pulled by impulse like a puppet on strings, from working through thoughts step by step, and from serving the body.
single.why: Only this passage says what death gives: rest from what has worked on me all my life. No other passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Death ends the blows on the senses, the pull of impulse, the step-by-step working of thought and the service of the body.

single.quote: if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child.
single.label: When I am afraid
single.t: If I am afraid of death, I am like a child afraid of a work of nature. The way back is to look at dying by itself and take apart what I have imagined into it, until I judge it to be nothing but a work of nature.
single.why: Only this passage says how to take the fear apart: look at dying by itself and remove what is imagined into it. 8.55 also speaks of fear, but argues by cases.
single.follows: Looked at by itself, with what was imagined into it taken away, dying is only a work of nature, and fearing it is childish.

single.quote: Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.
single.label: Either way
single.t: If I fear death, I fear either having no sensation or having a different kind. With none, I will sense nothing bad; with a different kind, I will be a different living thing and will not have stopped living.
single.why: Only this passage argues by both cases. It holds whatever death turns out to be, even if it is not the natural change the other passages describe, which is why it stands under doubt.
single.follows: Whatever death is, it brings either nothing to feel, so nothing bad, or a new kind of feeling and a life that goes on.

Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as
one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that
nature hath appointed. For what thou dost conceive of these, of a boy to
become a young man, to wax old, to grow, to ripen, to get teeth, or a
beard, or grey hairs to beget, to bear, or to be delivered; or what
other action soever it be, that is natural unto man according to the
several seasons of his life; such a thing is it also to be dissolved. It
is therefore the part of a wise man, in matter of death, not in any wise
to carry himself either violently, or proudly but patiently to wait for
it, as one of nature's operations: that with the same mind as now thou
dost expect when that which yet is but an embryo in thy wife's belly
shall come forth, thou mayst expect also when thy soul shall fall off
from that outward coat or skin: wherein as a child in the belly it lieth
involved and shut up. But thou desirest a more popular, and though not
so direct and philosophical, yet a very powerful and penetrative recipe
against the fear of death, nothing can make they more willing to part
with thy life, than if thou shalt consider, both what the subjects
themselves are that thou shalt part with, and what manner of disposition
thou shalt no more have to do with. True it is, that, offended with them
thou must not be by no means, but take care of them, and meekly bear
with them However, this thou mayst remember, that whensoever it happens
that thou depart, it shall not be from men that held the same opinions
that thou dost. For that indeed, (if it were so) is the only thing that
might make thee averse from death, and willing to continue here, if it
were thy hap to live with men that had obtained the same belief that
thou hast. But now, what a toil it is for thee to live with men of
different opinions, thou seest: so that thou hast rather occasion to
say, Hasten, I thee pray, O Death; lest I also in time forget myself.
members.english: Do not despise death, but be well pleased with it, since this too is one of the things nature wills. For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved. This, then, is what fits a human being who has reasoned it out: not to be offhand toward death, nor violent, nor disdainful, but to wait for it as one of the natural activities; and, as you now wait for the time when the unborn child will come out of your wife’s womb, in the same way to await the hour in which your little soul will drop out of this husk. But if you also want a layman’s rule that touches the heart, what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave, and [at what kind of] characters [your soul] will no longer be mixed up with. For there must be no taking offence at them at all; rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently, yet remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you. For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own. But as it is you see how much weariness there is in the discord of living together, so that one says: “Come sooner, death, in case I too should perhaps forget myself.”

members.text:
To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other
things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed
pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them
contemn death as much as any. And can death be terrible to him, to
whom that only seems good, which in the ordinary course of nature is
seasonable? to him, to whom, whether his actions be many or few, so they
be all good, is all one; and who whether he behold the things of the
world being always the same either for many years, or for few years
only, is altogether indifferent? O man! as a citizen thou hast lived,
and conversed in this great city the world. Whether just for so many
years, or no, what is it unto thee? Thou hast lived (thou mayest be
sure) as long as the laws and orders of the city required; which may be
the common comfort of all. Why then should it be grievous unto thee, if
(not a tyrant, nor an unjust judge, but) the same nature that brought
thee in, doth now send thee out of the world? As if the praetor should
fairly dismiss him from the stage, whom he had taken in to act a while.
Oh, but the play is not yet at an end, there are but three acts yet
acted of it? Thou hast well said: for in matter of life, three acts is
the whole play. Now to set a certain time to every man's acting, belongs
unto him only, who as first he was of thy composition, so is now the
cause of thy dissolution. As for thyself; thou hast to do with
neither. Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that
dismisseth thee.
members.english:
What most rouses one to despise death is that even those who judge pleasure good and pain bad have despised it all the same.

A person for whom only what comes at the right time is good, for whom performing more actions in line with right reason is equal to performing fewer, and to whom it makes no difference whether they look on the universe for a longer or a shorter time: to that person not even death is a thing to fear.

Man, you have been a citizen in this great city. What difference does it make to you whether for five years or for three? For what accords with the laws is equal for each. So what is terrible if you are sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in, just as if the magistrate who engaged a comic actor were to dismiss him from the stage? “But I have spoken not the five acts but the three.” Well said; in life, however, the three are the whole play. For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither. So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.

There is not any man that is so happy in his death, but that some
of those that are by him when he dies, will be ready to rejoice at his
supposed calamity. Is it one that was virtuous and wise indeed? will
there not some one or other be found, who thus will say to himself;
'Well now at last shall I be at rest from this pedagogue. He did not
indeed otherwise trouble us much: but I know well enough that in his
heart, he did much condemn us.' Thus will they speak of the virtuous.
But as for us, alas I how many things be there, for which there be many
that glad would be to be rid of us. This therefore if thou shalt think
of whensoever thou diest, thou shalt die the more willingly, when thou
shalt think with thyself; I am now to depart from that world, wherein
those that have been my nearest friends and acquaintances, they whom I
have so much suffered for, so often prayed for, and for whom I have
taken such care, even they would have me die, hoping that after my death
they shall live happier, than they did before. What then should any man
desire to continue here any longer? Nevertheless, whensoever thou diest,
thou must not be less kind and loving unto them for it; but as before,
see them, continue to be their friend, to wish them well, and meekly,
and gently to carry thyself towards them, but yet so that on the other
side, it make thee not the more unwilling to die. But as it fareth with
them that die an easy quick death, whose soul is soon separated from
their bodies, so must thy separation from them be. To these had nature
joined and annexed me: now she parts us; I am ready to depart, as from
friends and kinsmen, but yet without either reluctancy or compulsion.
For this also is according to Nature.
members.english: No one is so fortunate that, as they die, there will not be some people standing by who welcome the bad thing that is happening. Say the person was good and wise: may there not, at the very last, be someone who says to themselves: “Shall we at last get a breathing space from this minder? He was not hard on any of us, but I could feel that he was quietly condemning us.” That, then, in the case of the good person. But in our case how many other things there are on account of which many a person is longing to be rid of us! So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, took thought, those very people want me to go, hoping perhaps to get some other relief out of it. Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?” Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly toward them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious. And, on the other hand, not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, such too must the withdrawal from these people be. For nature tied you to these people too and put you together with them, but now it unties. I am being untied, as from my own people, it is true, yet not pulled back but without force; for this too is one of the things that accord with nature.
members.greek: Οὐδείς ἐστιν οὕτως εὔποτμος ᾧ ἀποθνῄσκοντι οὐ παρεστήξονταί τινες ἀσπαζόμενοι τὸ συμβαῖνον κακόν. σπουδαῖος καὶ σοφὸς ἦν· μὴ τὸ πανύστατον ἔσται τις ὁ καθ’ αὑτὸν λέγων· ἀναπνεύσομέν ποτε ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ; χαλεπὸς μὲν οὐδενὶ ἡμῶν ἦν, ἀλλὰ ᾐσθανόμην ὅτι ἡσυχῇ καταγινώσκει ἡμῶν. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τοῦ σπουδαίου, ἐφ’ ἡμῶν δὲ πόσα ἄλλα ἐστί, δι’ ἃ πολὺς ὁ ἀπαλλακτιῶν ἡμῶν. τοῦτο οὖν ἐννοήσεις ἀποθνῄσκων καὶ εὐκολώτερον ἐξελεύσῃ, λογιζόμενος· ἐκ τοιούτου βίου ἀπέρχομαι, ἐν ᾧ αὐτοὶ οἱ κοινωνοί, ὑπὲρ ὧν τὰ τοσαῦτα ἠγωνισάμην, ηὐξάμην, ἐφρόντισα, αὐτοὶ ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσί με ὑπάγειν, ἄλλην τινὰ τυχὸν ἐκ τούτου ῥᾳστώνην ἐλπίζοντες. τί ἂν οὖν τις ἀντέχοιτο τῆς ἐνταῦθα μακροτέρας διατριβῆς; μὴ μέντοι διὰ τοῦτο ἔλαττον εὐμενὴς αὐτοῖς ἄπιθι, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἴδιον ἔθος διασῴζων, φίλος καὶ εὔνους καὶ ἵλεως· καὶ μὴ πάλιν ὡς ἀποσπώμενος, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ εὐθανατοῦντος εὐκόλως τὸ ψυχάριον ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος ἐξειλεῖται, τοιαύτην καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τούτων ἀποχώρησιν δεῖ γίνεσθαι· καὶ γὰρ τούτοις ἡ φύσις συνῆψε καὶ συνέκρινεν, ἀλλὰ νῦν διαλύει. διαλύομαι ὡς ἀπὸ οἰκείων μέν, οὐ μὴν ἀνθελκόμενος ἀλλʼ ἀβιάστως· ἓν γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο τῶν κατὰ φύσιν.

members.text:
It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty, to
consider what they themselves are in very deed, from whose bare conceits
and voices, honour and credit do proceed: as also what it is to die, and
how if a man shall consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate
from it in his mind all those things which with it usually represent
themselves unto us, he can conceive of it no otherwise, than as of a
work of nature, and he that fears any work of nature, is a very child.
Now death, it is not only a work of nature, but also conducing to
nature.
members.english: To attend [to these things] belongs to the power of mind. What these people are, whose judgments and voices give a good name. What dying is, and that, if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child. This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.
members.greek: νοερᾶς δυνάμεως ἐφιστάναι. τί εἰσιν οὗτοι, ὧν αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι. τί ἐστι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ ὅτι, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ μόνον ἴδῃ καὶ τῷ μερισμῷ τῆς ἐννοίας διαλύσῃ τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ, οὐκέτι ἄλλο τι ὑπολήψεται αὐτὸ εἶναι ἢ φύσεως ἔργον· φύσεως δὲ ἔργον εἴ τις φοβεῖται, παιδίον ἐστί· τοῦτο μέντοι οὐ μόνον φύσεως ἔργον ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφέρον αὐτῇ.

members.text:
No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly
said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end. Neither can he that
is the author of that operation; for this very respect, because his
operation is at an end, be said to suffer any evil. Likewise then,
neither can the whole body of all our actions (which is our life) if in
time it cease, be said to suffer any evil for this very reason, because
it is at an end; nor he truly be said to have been ill affected, that
did put a period to this series of actions. Now this time or certain
period, depends of the determination of nature: sometimes of particular
nature, as when a man dieth old; but of nature in general, however; the
parts whereof thus changing one after another, the whole world still
continues fresh and new. Now that is ever best and most seasonable,
which is for the good of the whole. Thus it appears that death of
itself can neither be hurtful to any in particular, because it is not a
shameful thing (for neither is it a thing that depends of our own will,
nor of itself contrary to the common good) and generally, as it is both
expedient and seasonable to the whole, that in that respect it must
needs be good. It is that also, which is brought unto us by the order
and appointment of the Divine Providence; so that he whose will and
mind in these things runs along with the Divine ordinance, and by this
concurrence of his will and mind with the Divine Providence, is led
and driven along, as it were by God Himself; may truly be termed and
esteemed the θεοφόρητος, or divinely led and inspired.
members.english: Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped; nor has the one who did this action suffered anything bad just in this respect, that it has stopped. In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped; nor has the one who brought this chain to a stop at the right time been put in a bad state. The right time and the limit are given by nature: sometimes by one’s own nature too, when the stopping comes in old age, but in every case by the nature of the whole, with the changing of whose parts the entire universe stays always young and in its prime. And everything that benefits the whole is always fine and in season. So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole. For in this way a person is also carried by god: the one who is carried in the same way as god and is carried, in their purpose, toward the same things.
members.greek: Μία καὶ ἡτισοῦν ἐνέργεια κατὰ καιρὸν παυσαμένη οὐδὲν κακὸν πάσχει, καθὸ πέπαυται· οὐδὲ ὁ πράξας τὴν πρᾶξιν ταύτην κατ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καθὸ πέπαυται, κακόν τι πέπονθεν. ὁμοίως οὖν τὸ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πράξεων σύστημα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ βίος, ἐὰν ἐν καιρῷ παύσηται, οὐδὲν κακὸν πάσχει κατ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καθὸ πέπαυται· οὐδὲ ὁ καταπαύσας ἐν καιρῷ τὸν εἱρμὸν τοῦτον κακῶς διετέθη. τὸν δὲ καιρὸν καὶ τὸν ὅρον δίδωσιν ἡ φύσις, ποτὲ μὲν καὶ ἡ ἰδία, ὅταν ἐν γήρᾳ, πάντως δὲ ἡ τῶν ὅλων, ἧς τῶν μερῶν μεταβαλλόντων νεαρὸς ἀεὶ καὶ ἀκμαῖος ὁ σύμπας κόσμος διαμένει. καλὸν δὲ ἀεὶ πᾶν καὶ ὡραῖον τὸ συμφέρον τῷ ὅλῳ. ἡ οὖν κατάπαυσις τοῦ βίου ἑκάστῳ οὐ κακὸν μὲν ὅτι οὐδὲ αἰσχρόν, εἴπερ καὶ ἀπροαίρετον καὶ οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον· ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἴπερ τῷ ὅλῳ καίριον καὶ συμφέρον καὶ συμφερόμενον. οὕτως γὰρ καὶ θεοφόρητος ὁ φερόμενος κατὰ ταὐτὰ θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ ταὐτὰ τῇ γνώμῃ φερόμενος.

members.text:
Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an
action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from
opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the
death of it. In all this there is no hurt. Apply this now to a man's
age, as first, a child; then a youth, then a young man, then an old man;
every change from one age to another is a kind of death And all this
while here no matter of grief yet. Pass now unto that life first, that
which thou livedst under thy grandfather, then under thy mother, then
under thy father. And thus when through the whole course of thy life
hitherto thou hast found and observed many alterations, many changes,
many kinds of endings and cessations, put this question to thyself What
matter of grief or sorrow dost thou find in any of these? Or what doest
thou suffer through any of these? If in none of these, then neither
in the ending and consummation of thy whole life, which is also but a
cessation and change.
members.english: The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad. Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible? Now pass on to your life under your grandfather, then your life under your mother, then your life under your father; and as you find many other things perishing and changing and ending, ask yourself: “Surely that is nothing terrible?” In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.
members.greek: Ἐνεργείας ἀπόληξις, ὁρμῆς, ὑπολήψεως παῦλα καὶ οἷον θάνατος· οὐδὲν κακόν. μέτιθι νῦν ἐπὶ ἡλικίαν, οἷον τὴν παιδικήν, τὴν τοῦ μειρακίου, τὴν νεότητα, τὸ γῆρας· καὶ γὰρ τούτων πᾶσα μεταβολή, θάνατος· μήτι δεινόν; μέτιθι νῦν ἐπὶ βίον τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πάππῳ, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῇ μητρί, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πατρί, καὶ ἄλλας δὲ πολλὰς διαφθορὰς καὶ μεταβολὰς καὶ ἀπολήξεις εὑρίσκων ἐπερώτα σεαυτόν· μήτι δεινόν; οὕτως τοίνυν οὐδὲ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου σου βίου λῆξις καὶ παῦλα καὶ μεταβολή.

members.text:
He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at
all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather
comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil;
or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
members.english: Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.
members.greek: Ὁ τὸν θάνατον φοβούμενος ἤτοι ἀναισθησίαν φοβεῖται ἢ αἴσθησιν ἑτεροίαν. ἀλλ’ εἴτε οὐκέτι αἴσθησιν, οὐδὲ κακοῦ τινος αἰσθήσῃ· εἴτε ἀλλοιοτέραν αἴσθησιν κτήσῃ, ἀλλοῖον ζῷον ἔσῃ καὶ τοῦ ζῆν οὐ παύσῃ.

members.text:
Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the
tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of
the body.
members.english: Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.
members.greek: Θάνατος ἀνάπαυλα αἰσθητικῆς ἀντιτυπίας καὶ ὁρμητικῆς νευροσπαστίας καὶ διανοητικῆς διεξόδου καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὴν σάρκα λειτουργίας.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 12.27 is 12.34–36, 2.10 is 2.12b, 12.17 is 12.23, 9.19 is 9.21, 8.55 is 8.58 and 6.26 is 6.28, while 9.3 and 10.36 are the same.

Leaves out most of 12.27. Its middle paragraph (12.35: to someone for whom only what comes at the right time is good, and to whom a longer or shorter look at the universe makes no difference, not even death is a thing to fear), “five years or three” and the three acts turn on how long a life is, the subject of the section on the shortness of life (Article 35); claim 3 takes the right time from 12.17. Its first remark, that even those who judge pleasure good have despised death, is left out because its “despise death” pulls against 9.3’s “Do not despise death”, a tension the translators kept visible.

Reads “the one who was responsible then for the putting together” in 12.27 as nature, since the same passage has just named nature as the one who brought you in. The Greek word is masculine, so it may be god or the magistrate of the play image.

Leaves out the end of 9.3, “Come sooner, death, in case I too should perhaps forget myself”. It is a cry of weariness at living among people of other principles, not a way of meeting death, and the article does not turn it into a rule.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one: Article 10 (claim 4) that I wait for death cheerfully as a dissolving according to nature, so 9.3’s waiting is left to it; Article 17 that dying is one of the acts of my life, near claim 1; Article 33 that my death is a change of the same kind as my birth and that nature aimed at my ending (claims 3 and 4), and Article 32 that change is nothing bad for what is changed (claims 5 and 6), both near claim 2; Article 34 that I leave life with good grace (claim 6) and that death is an end or a move (claim 10, which 8.55 here says again); Article 6 that what comes is timely. What this section adds is the small deaths of my own ages and activities, the right time for the whole as the ground for calling death good, and above all how I leave the people of my life: graciously, not torn away, with goodwill, helped by seeing that nothing among them holds me. Claim 5 rests on a bleak view of those people that only two passages hold, and the article argues that death is not bad rather than proving it.
